title: A Gentle But Powerful Way To Increase Learning, Motivation, And Independence ning-motivation-and-independence/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin diagnoses the problem of students who freeze up during independent practice not as an ability gap but as learned helplessness caused by excessive teacher hovering. He argues that once a student passes checks for understanding, further hand-holding erodes their self-reliance and initiative rather than supporting learning. His proposed fix is a gradual, encouragement-based withdrawal: continuing to acknowledge raised hands but responding with verbal reassurance ('You can do it. I believe in you') instead of kneeling down to re-teach. Over time, this fading presence is meant to rebuild students' confidence and self-starter capacity while the teacher becomes a quiet observer watching for genuine need.
points: Students who freeze during independent practice often suffer from learned helplessness caused by excessive teacher support, not an inability to do the work.
If a student passes checks for understanding, hovering and reteaching afterward does more harm than good.
The fix is gradual: continuing to respond to raised hands, but with verbal encouragement instead of hands-on reteaching.
As the teacher fades into the background, hands in the air and requests for help should steadily decrease over time.
The teacher's ultimate role during independent practice becomes a quiet observer watching only for genuine signs of struggle.
quotes: So you teach this great lesson. Your students are really into it. They’re listening and participating.
You do for them what you know they can do for themselves. It’s exhausting, but you do it lesson after lesson and day after day

Their problem, you see, isn’t their inability. It’s not motivation, at least not directly. If they can pass your checks for understanding, then you’ve provided everything they need to work independently. The problem is learned helplessness.
Independence is a gift you give your students by gently withholding help for that which you know they can do themselves.
After finishing up a lesson, you’ll become a ghostly presence, neither ignoring nor helping, but just watching for signs of struggle
